analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to let workers earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill earned 33 Senate sponsors, none of them Republican, and never advanced past its first-day referral to committee; no vote was ever held in either chamber during the 2019-2021 Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would require employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (about seven workdays) a year. Workers could use the time for their own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, or domestic partner, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Employers with fewer than 15 workers could opt out of the paid requirement but would then have to provide the same 56 hours unpaid. The bill would bar employers from firing or penalizing workers for using the leave, and would let the Labor Department investigate complaints and let workers sue to enforce their rights.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of workers who lack paid sick time, concentrated among low-wage workers. By the bill's own findings, 55 percent of private-sector workers in the lowest wage quartile lack paid sick time, along with more than 80 percent of food-preparation and serving workers, over half of Latino workers, and nearly half of Native American or Alaskan Native workers. Workers facing domestic violence would gain protected time off to seek medical care, counseling, relocation, or court action. Employers also gain in limited ways: fewer workers coming to work sick (presenteeism costs an estimated $308 billion a year in lost productivity) and reduced spread of contagious illness on the job.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers without paid sick leave

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees must provide at least one hour of earned paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year.

The time can be used for the worker's own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, domestic partner, or close relative, or to address domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.
It is unlawful for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny a worker's right to accrue sick leave, and workers may sue and the Department of Labor must investigate complaints of violations.

The bill's findings cite research that paid sick time laws reduced population influenza rates by 5.5 to 6.5 percent in seven cities and that a universal policy would save about $1.1 billion a year, including $500 million for Medicare and Medicaid, through fewer preventable emergency-room visits.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who bear the cost of paid leave for hours not worked. The cost falls hardest on industries where workers currently lack sick leave, such as food service and retail, since higher-wage employers generally already provide comparable leave and can count existing policies toward the requirement. Very small employers under 15 workers can shift the cost to workers themselves by providing the 56 hours unpaid.

drawbacks.text: Employers with fewer than 15 employees may opt out of paying for the leave and instead provide the same 56 hours unpaid, meaning workers at small businesses could get time off with no income to cover the absence.

The bill imposes a new wage cost on employers in sectors with thin margins, and requires record-keeping, posted notices, and compliance with certification rules, including possible doctor's notes for absences longer than three consecutive workdays.
The benefit is capped at 56 hours a year and workers must wait 60 calendar days after being hired before they can use any earned time, so new employees remain uncovered for their first two months.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 29 percent of private-sector workers who lack any paid sick time, the benefit is direct: income protection during illness, the ability to see a doctor or care for a sick child without losing pay, and protection from retaliation. The costs fall on employers, mostly in low-wage service industries, and the bill narrows them with a 56-hour cap, a small-employer carve-out, and credit for existing leave policies. The main design weakness is the small-employer opt-out to unpaid leave, which gives the smallest businesses' workers time off without pay, and the 60-day waiting period for new hires.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill, read it twice, and sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day, and the committee never held a markup or hearing on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill in the Senate on March 14, 2019.
That same day the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action of any kind was taken: the committee never reported the bill, and neither the Senate nor the House ever voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
Thirty-three senators sponsored or cosponsored the bill, 31 Democrats and 2 independents; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers without paid sick leave obligations, particularly in low-wage food service and retail sectors, are better off because the bill never moved: no leave mandate was enacted. The 29 percent of private-sector workers who lack paid sick time gained nothing; they remain able to be fired or lose income for staying home sick.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers with no sick leave mandate

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act in the Senate and recruited 32 additional cosponsors.

for.name: 33 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 33 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; no markup or hearing on it was ever scheduled during his tenure.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business groups
against.role: Opponents of federal paid sick leave mandates
against.what_they_did: Opposed and lobbied against federal paid sick leave mandates as a cost to employers.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or independent (31 Democrats and 2 independents); no Republican signed on, and the Republican-chaired committee that received the bill took no action.

industries.industry: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: These industries have the least access to paid sick time among their workforces (over 80 percent of food-preparation and serving workers lack it), so the mandate would impose the largest new wage cost here. The bill's interest runs directly against these employers' current practice of saving money by not paying workers who stay home sick.

The bill lets them opt out of the paid requirement and provide the 56 hours unpaid, avoiding most of the cost, though they still face record-keeping and notice duties. Their workers get time off without pay unless the employer volunteers to pay.

industries.industry: Larger employers with existing generous leave policies
industries.note: Employers whose existing paid leave policies already meet the bill's amount and purposes need not add anything, so the bill levels the playing field against competitors that offer no paid leave. Presenteeism-related productivity losses cited at $308 billion a year also fall partly on these employers.
